questions.question: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act (1992) aimed at legal reform in which of the following areas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Local self-governance at rural level**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992** was a landmark legislation in India aimed at decentralizing power and establishing **local self-governance at the rural level**. It provided a constitutional foundation for the **Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)**. *Hence, statement 3 is correct.*
 
• The act added a new **Part IX** to the **Constitution of India**, titled **The Panchayats**, which consists of provisions from **Article 243 to 243-O**. It also introduced the **Eleventh Schedule**, which lists **29 functional items** that are placed under the care of the Panchayats.
 
• **Industrial disputes management** is primarily governed by the **Industrial Disputes Act, 1947**, which focuses on the investigation and settlement of industrial conflicts between employers and workmen. It is not the subject of the 73rd Amendment. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.*
 
• **Environmental protection at the grassroot level** is addressed through various laws like the **Environment Protection Act, 1986** and the **Forest Rights Act, 2006**. While Panchayats have some roles in social forestry, the 73rd Amendment's primary legal reform was the institutionalization of the governance structure itself. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*
 
• **Consumer protection rights** are regulated by the **Consumer Protection Act, 1986** (later replaced by the **2019 Act**), which establishes consumer councils and authorities for the settlement of disputes. This is unrelated to the structural reform of rural local bodies. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Historical Background:** The **73rd Amendment Act** was passed during the tenure of **Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao**. It came into force on **April 24, 1993**. This date is now commemorated annually as **National Panchayati Raj Day** in India.
 
• **Three-Tier System:** The Act mandates a uniform **three-tier structure** of Panchayati Raj across the country: the **Gram Panchayat** at the village level, the **Panchayat Samiti** at the intermediate (block) level, and the **Zila Parishad** at the district level. States with a population below **20 lakh** have the option not to constitute the intermediate level.
 
• **Gram Sabha:** The Act establishes the **Gram Sabha** as the foundation of the Panchayati Raj system. It is a body consisting of all persons registered in the electoral rolls of a village within the area of the Panchayat.
 
• **Reservation of Seats:** To ensure social justice, the Act provides for the **reservation of seats** for **Scheduled Castes (SCs)** and **Scheduled Tribes (STs)** in proportion to their population. Most importantly, it mandates that **not less than one-third (33%)** of the total number of seats and offices of chairpersons must be reserved for **women**.
 
• **Duration and Elections:** Every Panchayat is given a fixed tenure of **5 years**. In case of dissolution, elections must be held within a period of **6 months**. The minimum age for contesting elections to Panchayats is **21 years**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **State Election Commission:** The Act provides for the constitution of a **State Election Commission** in every state. This independent body is responsible for the superintendence, direction, and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of all **elections to the Panchayats**.
 
• **State Finance Commission:** To ensure the financial viability of these local bodies, the **Governor** of a state is required to constitute a **State Finance Commission** every **5 years**. This commission reviews the financial position of the Panchayats and recommends the principles for the distribution of **net proceeds of taxes** between the State and the Panchayats.
 
• **Eleventh Schedule Subjects:** The **29 subjects** transferred to the Panchayats include **Agriculture**, **Land Improvement**, **Minor Irrigation**, **Animal Husbandry**, **Fisheries**, **Social Forestry**, **Small Scale Industries**, **Rural Housing**, **Drinking Water**, and **Education**.
 
• **Article 40:** The 73rd Amendment gave practical shape to **Article 40** of the **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**, which directs the State to organize village panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as units of **self-government**.

questions.question: India recently became the fourth country to successfully demonstrate space docking. Which of the following countries had achieved this feat before India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**USA, Russia, China**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **India** has achieved a major milestone in its space exploration journey by becoming the **fourth country** in the world to successfully demonstrate **space docking** technology.

• **Space docking** is a complex maneuver where two independently launched spacecraft are joined together in orbit to form a single unit. This is essential for transferring crew, fuel, or cargo.

• Before India, only the **United States (USA)**, **Russia** (formerly the Soviet Union), and **China** had mastered this critical technology.

• The **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** conducted this demonstration through the **SPADEX** (Space Docking Experiment) mission, which involved two satellites (a Chaser and a Target) meeting and joining in space.

• This capability is a prerequisite for India's future ambitious projects, including the **Bharatiya Antariksh Station** (India's own space station) and the **Gaganyaan** mission's advanced phases.

**Additional Information__**

• The first-ever manual space docking was performed by the **USA** in **1966** during the **Gemini 8** mission, piloted by **Neil Armstrong** and **David Scott**.

• The **Soviet Union** achieved the first fully automated docking in **1967** using the **Cosmos 186** and **Cosmos 188** spacecraft.

• **China** became the third nation to achieve independent docking capability in **2011** with the **Shenzhou 8** and **Tiangong-1** mission.

• Mastering docking technology allows for **satellite servicing**, **refueling in orbit**, and **deep-space exploration** missions where multiple components must be assembled in space.

• India aims to establish its own space station by the year **2035** and land an Indian on the **Moon** by **2040**.
</ul

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Polaris Dawn Mission and Van Allen Radiation Belts:**1. The Van Allen Belts consist of charged particles originating exclusively from the Sun.
2. The Polaris Dawn Mission studied the biological effects of space radiation by traveling through high-radiation zones around Earth.
3. Spacecraft passing through the Van Allen Belts must limit their transit time to reduce radiation exposure.
Which of the above statements is/are correct**?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2 and 3 only**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Statement 1 is incorrect:** The **Van Allen Radiation Belts** are two donut-shaped regions of energetic charged particles (protons and electrons) trapped by Earth's magnetic field. While a significant portion of these particles originates from the **Solar Wind** (the Sun), they also come from **Cosmic Rays** originating from outside the solar system. Therefore, they do not originate exclusively from the Sun.

• **Statement 2 is correct:** The **Polaris Dawn Mission**, a private spaceflight mission operated by **SpaceX**, was specifically designed to reach a high-altitude orbit (with an apogee of approximately 1,400 kilometers). This trajectory allowed the crew to pass through portions of the **Van Allen belts** to conduct research on the **biological effects of space radiation** on the human body, which is crucial for future long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars.

• **Statement 3 is correct:** Due to the high intensity of ionizing radiation within the **Van Allen Belts**, spacecraft and their crews are at risk of radiation sickness and electronic failure. To mitigate these risks, mission planners ensure that spacecraft pass through these zones as **quickly as possible** to minimize the total **cumulative radiation dose**.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Polaris Dawn** mission featured the first-ever **commercial spacewalk** (Extravehicular Activity or EVA) conducted by private citizens.

• The mission utilized the **SpaceX Crew Dragon** spacecraft and reached the highest Earth orbit for a crewed mission since the **Apollo program**.

• The **Van Allen belts** were discovered in 1958 by **James Van Allen** using data from the **Explorer 1** satellite, which was the first U.S. satellite.

• The **Inner Belt** mostly contains high-energy protons, while the **Outer Belt** is primarily composed of high-energy electrons.
</ul

questions.question: The Rigveda points to an organized society. What kind of marriage existed there?

options.text: Both monogamy and polygamy was practiced equally
Monogamy was general rule but some princes practiced polygamy

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Monogamy was general rule but some princes practiced polygamy**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Rigveda**, which is the oldest of the four **Vedas**, provides a glimpse into the social structure of the **Early Vedic Period** (circa **1500 BCE to 1000 BCE**). In this society, **Monogamy** (the practice of having one spouse at a time) was the established general rule for the vast majority of the population. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• While **Monogamy** was the social norm, **Polygamy** (the practice of having more than one wife) was prevalent among the ruling classes, such as **Princes**, **Kings**, and noble **Kshatriyas**. This was often done for political alliances or to ensure multiple heirs. ***Hence, statement 4 is correct.***

• The idea that only **Polygamy** was practiced is historically inaccurate, as the **Rigvedic** hymns frequently celebrate the union of a single husband and wife as a sacred and stable unit of the **Kula** (family). ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

• **Monogamy** and **Polygamy** were not practiced equally; **Monogamy** was the standard for the common **Aryans** (Vis), whereas **Polygamy** was an exception reserved for the elite. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• The **Rigvedic** society was **Patriarchal**, meaning the head of the family was the **Kulapa** (usually the father), but women enjoyed a high status and participated in religious sacrifices alongside their husbands.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Status of Women:** Women in the **Rigvedic** period were not secluded. They received education and some even composed hymns, known as **Brahmavadinis**. Famous examples include **Lopamudra**, **Ghosha**, **Viswavara**, and **Apala**.

• **Marriage Customs:** **Child marriage** was virtually non-existent during this era. Girls were usually married at a mature age, typically between **16 and 17 years**. The **Rigveda** mentions the **Vahatu**, which were gifts given to the bride by her parents, often considered a precursor to the **Dowry** system.

• **Widow Remarriage:** The practice of **Niyoga** (levirate marriage) existed, where a childless widow could marry her **Devar** (younger brother-in-law) to produce a son for the deceased husband's lineage. This indicates a pragmatic approach to family continuity.

• **Types of Union:** While formal marriages were the norm, the **Rigveda** also alludes to **Gandharva Vivaha** (love marriage) and mentions the **Svayamvara** (where a woman chooses her husband), though these became more structured in the **Later Vedic Period**.

• **Social Units:** The basic unit of society was the **Kula** (family). Multiple families formed a **Grama** (village), led by a **Gramani**. A group of villages formed a **Vis** (clan), and the highest political unit was the **Jana** (tribe), headed by a **Rajan** (King).

**Important Points__**

• **Geographical Location:** The **Rigvedic** people lived in the **Saptasindhu** region, which refers to the land of the seven rivers, including the **Indus** (Sindhu), **Vitasta** (Jhelum), **Asikni** (Chenab), **Parushni** (Ravi), **Vipas** (Beas), **Sutudri** (Sutlej), and the **Saraswati**.

• **Religious Significance:** Marriage was viewed as a **Sacrament** rather than a contract. The **Surya-Savitri** hymn in the **10th Mandala** of the **Rigveda** provides the earliest description of wedding rituals, many of which are still followed in **Hindu** weddings today.

• **Polyandry:** There is very little evidence of **Polyandry** (one wife, multiple husbands) in the **Rigveda**, although some scholars point to the mythological story of the **Maruts** and **Rodasi** or the **Ashvins** marrying **Surya** as rare allegorical exceptions.

• **Economic Life:** The **Rigvedic** society was primarily **Pastoral**. **Cattle** (Gau) was the most valued possession and often served as a medium of exchange. The term for a daughter, **Duhitri**, literally means 'one who milks the cow'.
</ul

questions.question: Which plant tissue is primarily responsible for forming the hard husk of a coconut?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sclerenchyma**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
__

• **Sclerenchyma** is the permanent plant tissue that makes the plant hard and stiff. The **husk of a coconut** is made of sclerenchymatous tissue.

• The cells of **Sclerenchyma** tissue are **dead**, long, and narrow. They lack a nucleus and cytoplasm at maturity.

• The cell walls are greatly thickened with **lignin**, a chemical substance that acts as cement and hardens them, providing structural rigidity.

• **Parenchyma** consists of living cells with thin cell walls and is primarily responsible for **food storage** and photosynthesis. It is the most common simple permanent tissue.

• **Collenchyma** provides **flexibility** and mechanical support to plant parts like the petiole and young stems, allowing them to bend without breaking.

• **Xylem** is a complex permanent tissue responsible for the **conduction of water** and minerals from the roots to the leaves.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Sclerenchyma** tissue is found in stems, around vascular bundles, in the veins of leaves, and in the hard covering of **seeds and nuts**.

• There are two main types of sclerenchyma cells: **Fibers** (elongated cells often used commercially in making ropes and mats) and **Sclereids** (short, thick cells that give the gritty texture to fruits like pears).

• **Lignin** deposition is so thick in some sclerenchyma cells that there is no internal space (lumen) left inside the cell.

• Plant tissues are broadly classified into **Meristematic tissues** (capable of cell division) and **Permanent tissues** (mature cells that have lost the ability to divide).
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following was a key feature of India's trade policy reforms in 1991 period?

options.text: Imposing new quantitative restrictions on essential imports
Expanding import licensing to control foreign trade
Introducing quotas to limit agricultural exports
Removal of licensing procedures for imports

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Removal of licensing procedures for imports**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **1991 Trade Policy Reforms** were a fundamental part of the **New Economic Policy (NEP)**, which aimed to transition the **Indian economy** from a closed, state-controlled system to an open, market-oriented one.

• **Removal of licensing procedures for imports**: Prior to **1991**, India operated under a rigid **License-Permit Raj** where almost all imports required prior government approval. The **1991 reforms** abolished **import licensing** for the majority of goods, except for those that were **environmentally sensitive** or **hazardous**. This allowed industries to easily acquire **raw materials** and **capital goods** from abroad. **Hence, statement 4 is correct.**

• **Abolition of Quantitative Restrictions (QRs)**: The reforms focused on removing **quotas** and physical limits on the volume of imports. Imposing new quantitative restrictions would have contradicted the goal of **Liberalization**. **Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.**

• **Dismantling Trade Barriers**: Instead of expanding **import licensing** to control trade, the government sought to reduce administrative hurdles and eliminate discretionary controls that hindered **foreign trade**. **Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.**

• **Promotion of Agricultural Exports**: The policy aimed to integrate **Indian agriculture** with the global market by reducing **export duties** and removing restrictive **quotas**, rather than introducing new limits on exports. **Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.**

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Balance of Payments (BoP) Crisis**: In **1991**, India faced a severe **BoP crisis** where **foreign exchange reserves** plummeted to approximately **$1.2 billion**, barely enough to sustain **two weeks** of essential imports. This crisis was the primary catalyst for the structural reforms.

• **LPG Framework**: The reforms were built on the pillars of **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG)**. **Liberalization** involved the removal of government regulations to allow private players and market forces to determine economic outcomes.

• **Tariff Rationalization**: Before the reforms, India had some of the highest **customs duties** in the world, often exceeding **200%**. Post-**1991**, these **tariffs** were systematically reduced to make the **Indian industry** more competitive and reduce the cost of production.

• **Exchange Rate Reform**: In **July 1991**, the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** devalued the **Indian Rupee** by nearly **18-20%** against major global currencies. This move was intended to boost **exports** by making them cheaper and discourage **imports** by making them more expensive.

• **Role of IMF and World Bank**: The **1991 reforms** were part of the **Structural Adjustment Program** mandated by the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** and the **World Bank** in exchange for a **$7 billion** bailout loan to prevent a sovereign default.

**Important Points__**

• **New Industrial Policy 1991**: This policy accompanied trade reforms and abolished **industrial licensing** for all but **18 industries** (later reduced further), allowing for greater **private sector** participation and **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)**.

• **Foreign Trade Policy (FTP)**: The reforms shifted India from an **inward-looking** (import substitution) strategy to an **outward-looking** (export-led) growth strategy, significantly increasing India's share in **global trade**.

• **WTO Membership**: The liberalization of the trade regime prepared India for its role as a founding member of the **World Trade Organization (WTO)** in **1995**, committing the nation to international standards of **trade facilitation** and **non-tariff barrier** removal.

• **Key Figures**: The reforms were spearheaded by the then **Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao** and **Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh**, who are widely credited with saving the **Indian economy** from collapse and setting it on a high-growth trajectory.

• **Current Account Convertibility**: Following the **1991 reforms**, India moved towards **full convertibility** of the **Rupee** on the **current account** by **1994**, allowing for the free flow of funds for trade in goods and services.
</ul

questions.question: The first Five-Year Plan of India was launched in which year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1951**__.

**__Key Points__**

• The **First Five-Year Plan** of **India** was officially launched in the year **1951**. It was presented to the **Parliament** by the first Prime Minister of India, **Jawaharlal Nehru**. This plan laid the foundation for economic development in independent India. **Hence, the correct answer is 1951.**

• The plan was primarily based on the **Harrod-Domar model**, which emphasized the role of savings and investments in achieving economic growth. It was designed to address the immediate problems of **food shortage**, **inflation**, and the influx of refugees following the **Partition of India** in **1947**.

• The duration of the **First Five-Year Plan** was from **1951 to 1956**. Its main focus was on the **agricultural sector**, including investments in dams and irrigation. For instance, the construction of the **Bhakra-Nangal Dam** and the **Hirakud Dam** was initiated during this period.

• The target growth rate for the plan was set at 2.1%

questions.question: Who hand-calligraphed the original manuscript of the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Prem Behari Narain Raizada**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Prem Behari Narain Raizada** (Saxena) was the master calligrapher who hand-wrote the original manuscript of the **Constitution of India**. He belonged to a family of traditional calligraphers and learned the art from his grandfather.

• The original **Constitution** was not printed or typed; it was entirely **handwritten** in a flowing **italic style**. Raizada performed this monumental task in a room in **Constitution House** (now known as **Samvidhan Sadan**).

• When **Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru** approached him to write the document and asked about his fee, Raizada famously replied that he did not want a single penny. His only condition was that he be allowed to write his name on every page and his grandfather's name on the last page.

• He used approximately **432 pen nibs** (specifically **No. 303 nibs**) to complete the calligraphy of the **English** and **Hindi** versions. The entire process took about **six months** to finish.

• **B.N. Rau** (Sir Benegal Narsing Rau) served as the **Constitutional Advisor** to the **Constituent Assembly** and prepared the initial draft. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect regarding calligraphy.*

• **S.N. Mukherjee** was the **Chief Draftsman** of the Constitution and was praised for his ability to put complex proposals into legal shape. *Hence, statement 3 is incorrect regarding calligraphy.*

• **Gopalaswami Ayyangar** was a key member of the **Drafting Committee** and played a significant role in drafting **Article 370**. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect regarding calligraphy.*

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Artistic Decoration**: While Raizada did the calligraphy, the task of decorating and illuminating the pages was entrusted to artists from **Shantiniketan**. This team was led by **Nandalal Bose**.

• **Beohar Rammanohar Sinha**: He was a student of **Nandalal Bose** and is credited with the beautiful artwork on the **Preamble** page. His signature 'Ram' can be seen on the Preamble page.

• **Preservation**: The original handwritten copies of the Constitution (one in **English** and one in **Hindi**) are kept in special **helium-filled cases** in the **Library of the Parliament of India** in **New Delhi** to prevent deterioration.

• **Language**: The Constitution was originally written in both **Hindi** and **English**. Every member of the **Constituent Assembly** signed both copies on **January 24, 1950**.

• **Length**: The **Indian Constitution** is the **longest written constitution** of any sovereign nation in the world. At its inception, it contained **395 Articles**, **22 Parts**, and **8 Schedules**.

**Important Points__**

• **Drafting Committee**: Chaired by **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**, who is known as the **Father of the Indian Constitution**. The committee was responsible for scrutinizing the draft prepared by the **Constitutional Advisor**.

• **Timeline**: The **Constituent Assembly** took exactly **2 years, 11 months, and 18 days** to complete the final draft of the Constitution.

• **Adoption and Enforcement**: The Constitution was adopted on **November 26, 1949** (celebrated as **Constitution Day** or **Samvidhan Divas**), and it came into full legal force on **January 26, 1950**.

• **Sovereignty**: With the commencement of the Constitution, the **Indian Independence Act of 1947** and the **Government of India Act of 1935** were repealed, and India became a **Republic**.
</ul

questions.question: Identify the correct option base on given statements:**Assertion (A):** The Union Government alone can legislate on matters related to the deployment and jurisdiction of armed forces within Indian states.**Reason (R):** The Constitution includes the deployment of Union forces in aid of civil power, regulation of cantonments, and control over arms and atomic energy in the Union List

options.text: A and R are correct, and R is the correct reason for A
A and R both true, but R is not the appropriate explanation for A
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A and R are correct, and R is the correct reason for A**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **Assertion (A)** states that the **Union Government** alone has the authority to legislate on matters concerning the deployment and jurisdiction of **armed forces** within **Indian states**. Under **Article 246** of the **Constitution of India**, the **Parliament** has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in **List I** of the **Seventh Schedule**. Hence, statement **A** is correct.

• **Reason (R)** explains that the **Constitution** includes the deployment of **Union forces** in aid of civil power, regulation of **cantonments**, and control over **arms** and **atomic energy** in the **Union List**. These subjects are specifically mentioned under **Entry 2A**, **Entry 3**, **Entry 5**, and **Entry 6** of the **Union List** respectively. Hence, statement **R** is correct.

• The **Union List** (List I) is a list of **100 items** (originally 97) over which the **Union Government** or the **Parliament of India** has exclusive jurisdiction. Because the subjects mentioned in the reason are part of this list, the **Union** alone can legislate on them, which directly justifies the assertion.

• The deployment of **armed forces** in aid of civil power (**Entry 2A**) was notably inserted by the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, ensuring that the **Union** can assist states in maintaining public order while retaining legislative control over those forces.

• Since the legislative competence for the subjects in **Reason (R)** belongs solely to the **Union**, it provides the legal basis for the claim made in **Assertion (A)**. Hence, the correct answer is **A and R are correct, and R is the correct reason for A**.

**Additional Information__**

• **Seventh Schedule**: This schedule of the **Indian Constitution** provides for the distribution of powers and responsibilities between the **Union** and the **States**. It contains three lists: the **Union List**, the **State List**, and the **Concurrent List**.

• **Union List (List I)**: It includes subjects of national importance that require a uniform law across the **country**. Examples include **Defense** (Entry 1), **Foreign Affairs** (Entry 10), **Railways** (Entry 22), **Banking** (Entry 45), and **Census** (Entry 69).

• **Cantonments (Entry 3)**: The **Union** is responsible for the delimitation of **cantonment areas** and the constitution and powers of **cantonment authorities**. This ensures that military stations are governed by federal regulations rather than varying state laws.

• **Arms and Atomic Energy**: **Entry 5** covers **arms, firearms, ammunition, and explosives**, while **Entry 6** covers **atomic energy** and mineral resources necessary for its production. These are kept under **Union** control for **national security** and **strategic interests**.

• **Article 248 (Residuary Powers)**: The **Parliament** has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the **Concurrent List** or **State List**. This reinforces the **Union's** legislative supremacy in **India**.

• **Role of the President**: While the **Parliament** legislates, the **President of India** is the **Supreme Commander** of the **Armed Forces** under **Article 53(2)**, though the exercise of this power is regulated by law.
</ul

questions.question: According to the EIU, which country showed the most significant improvement in its business environment over the past 20 years?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vietnam**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• According to the **Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU)** Business Environment Rankings, **Vietnam** has demonstrated the most significant improvement in its business environment globally over the past **20 years**. This reflects the country's successful transition from a centrally planned economy to a market-oriented one.

• The **EIU**'s ranking is based on **91 indicators** across **11 categories**, including **political environment**, **macroeconomic stability**, **market potential**, **taxation**, and **infrastructure**. **Vietnam**'s score increased more than any other of the **82 countries** tracked in the long-term index.

• A primary driver for this improvement is **Vietnam**'s aggressive pursuit of **Free Trade Agreements (FTAs)**. The country is a member of the **Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP)** and has signed a landmark trade deal with the **European Union (EVFTA)**, which has drastically reduced tariffs and trade barriers.

• The **China Plus One** strategy adopted by multinational corporations has significantly benefited **Vietnam**. Companies looking to diversify their **manufacturing** bases away from **China** due to rising costs and geopolitical tensions have found **Vietnam** to be an ideal alternative due to its **strategic location** and competitive **labor costs**.

• While **India**, **Romania**, and **Serbia** have also shown notable improvements in their business climates, they did not match the consistent and comprehensive upward trajectory of **Vietnam** over the full **two-decade** period analyzed by the **EIU**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Doi Moi** reforms, initiated in **1986**, were the catalyst for **Vietnam**'s economic transformation, allowing for private enterprise and encouraging **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)**.

• **Vietnam**'s **GDP growth** has consistently been among the highest in **Southeast Asia**, often exceeding **6%** annually, driven by the **electronics**, **textiles**, and **footwear** manufacturing sectors.

• The **EIU** report highlights that **Vietnam**'s improvement is not just about low costs but also about **policy stability** and a government that is increasingly responsive to the needs of international investors.

• In the most recent **2023-2024** updates, other top improvers include **Thailand** and **India**, with **India** benefiting from its **digital infrastructure** boom and **Production Linked Incentive (PLI)** schemes.

questions.question: What does the fertility rate measure?

options.text: Number of live births per 1000 people in the population
Number of women in the population between ages 15 and 49
Number of live births per 1000 women aged 15 to 49 in a given year
Number of children born per family regardless of age

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Number of live births per 1000 women aged 15 to 49 in a given year**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **fertility rate**, specifically the **General Fertility Rate (GFR)**, is a demographic measure that calculates the **number of live births per 1000 women** of reproductive age in a specific **year**. This measure is more precise than the crude birth rate because it focuses only on the segment of the population capable of childbearing. *Hence, statement 3 is correct.*
 
• The **Crude Birth Rate (CBR)** is defined as the **number of live births per 1000 people** in the total population. Unlike the fertility rate, it includes men, children, and elderly women who are not in the reproductive age bracket, making it a broader but less refined indicator of fertility. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.*
 
• The **number of women in the population between ages 15 and 49** refers to the size of the **reproductive age group** or the **childbearing population**. While this data is essential for calculating fertility rates, the count itself is a demographic stock value and not a rate of birth. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*
 
• The **number of children born per family** is a concept related to **family size** or **completed fertility** at a micro-level. However, in formal **demography**, the fertility rate is standardized per 1000 women to allow for comparisons across different regions and time periods, rather than being measured simply per household or family. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Total Fertility Rate (TFR)**: This is the average number of children a woman would have by the end of her reproductive years if she were to experience the current **age-specific fertility rates**. It is one of the most widely used indicators to track population trends globally.
 
• **Replacement Level Fertility**: This is the specific **TFR** at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next without migration. In most **countries**, this value is considered to be **2.1**.
 
• **India's Fertility Trends**: According to the **National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5)** conducted between **2019 and 2021**, India's **TFR** has declined to **2.0**, which is below the **replacement level**. This indicates a significant shift in the **country's** demographic trajectory.
 
• **Age-Specific Fertility Rate (ASFR)**: This measures the **number of live births per 1000 women** within specific age cohorts, such as **20 to 24 years** or **25 to 29 years**. It helps **governments** and **organisations** understand at what **age** childbearing is most concentrated in a society.
 
• **Factors Affecting Fertility**: Several socio-economic **features** influence these rates, including **female literacy**, **age at marriage**, economic status, and the availability of **contraception** and **healthcare** services.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fecundity vs. Fertility**: In **demography**, **fecundity** refers to the biological potential or physical capacity to conceive, whereas **fertility** refers to the actual production of **live births**. A woman may be fecund but have zero fertility if she chooses not to have children.
 
• **Demographic Transition Model**: High **fertility rates** are typically observed in the early stages of the **Demographic Transition Model**, often seen in **developing nations**. As a **country** industrialises and **education** improves, it moves toward lower **birth rates** and **death rates**.
 
• **Global Context**: Many **developed countries** in **Europe** and **East Asia**, such as **Japan** and **South Korea**, are currently experiencing 'ultra-low' **fertility rates** (below **1.5**), leading to concerns about **ageing populations** and a shrinking **workforce**.

questions.question: The basic layout of early temples mentioned in the passage typically included:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dome, Garbhagriha, Pillars**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Garbhagriha**, which literally translates to **'womb-house'**, is the most essential part of an early temple. It is a small, square, and windowless chamber that houses the **main deity** or the **idol**. In the earliest stages of temple architecture, such as during the **Gupta Period**, the **Garbhagriha** was a simple room with a single entrance, designed to provide a secluded space for worship. ***Hence, this component is a correct part of the basic layout.***

• **Pillars** were fundamental structural elements used to support the **Mandapa** (assembly hall) or the entrance porch of the temple. Early structural temples, like **Temple 17 at Sanchi** (dating to the **5th Century CE**), featured a flat roof supported by four sturdy **pillars**. These **pillars** often had elaborate carvings and served both functional and aesthetic purposes in early temple design. ***Hence, this component is a correct part of the basic layout.***

• The **Dome** (or the early **Shikhara**) refers to the superstructure built over the **Garbhagriha**. While the very first temples had flat roofs, they soon evolved to include a pyramidal or curvilinear tower to signify the sacredness of the space. In early architectural contexts, the rounded crowning element or the **Amalaka** atop the spire gave it a **dome-like** appearance, distinguishing the temple from secular buildings. ***Hence, this component is a correct part of the basic layout.***

• The combination of a **Sanctum (Garbhagriha)**, **Pillars** for the porch, and a **Superstructure (Dome/Shikhara)** established the standard architectural vocabulary for Indian temples that would persist for centuries.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Nagara Style**: This style of temple architecture is primarily found in **North India**. Its most prominent feature is the **Shikhara**, which is a beehive-shaped tower that curves inward. The **Kandariya Mahadeva Temple** at **Khajuraho** is a classic example of this style, featuring multiple **mini-shikharas**.

• **Dravida Style**: Prevalent in **South India**, this style is characterized by a pyramid-shaped tower called a **Vimana**. These temples are often enclosed within high boundary walls with massive gateways known as **Gopurams**. The **Shore Temple** at **Mahabalipuram** is one of the earliest examples of **Dravidian architecture**.

• **Mandapa**: This is the **assembly hall** where devotees gather for prayers and rituals. In larger temples, there can be multiple **Mandapas** (such as the **Maha Mandapa** and **Ardha Mandapa**) leading toward the **Garbhagriha**.

• **Pradakshina Patha**: A **circumambulatory path** that allows devotees to walk around the **Garbhagriha** in a clockwise direction. This path can be open (**Nirandhara**) or enclosed (**Sandhara**).

**Important Points__**

• **Gupta Architecture**: The **Gupta Dynasty** (**4th to 6th Century CE**) marked the transition from **rock-cut caves** to **freestanding structural temples**. The **Dashavatara Temple** at **Deogarh** is significant as it is one of the earliest temples to feature a **Shikhara**.

• **Vesara Style**: This is a **hybrid style** that combines features of both **Nagara** and **Dravida** architecture. It was popularized by the **Chalukyas of Badami** and the **Hoysalas** in the **Deccan region**.

• **Jagati**: Many early temples were built on a **raised platform** called a **Jagati**, which elevated the sacred structure above the ground level.

• **Amalaka and Kalasha**: The **Amalaka** is a stone disc with ridges on the rim that sits atop the **Shikhara**, and the **Kalasha** is the pot-like finial that crowns the entire structure.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-renewable resource?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Coal**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Non-renewable resources** are natural resources that exist in a fixed amount and cannot be replaced by natural means at a pace quick enough to keep up with consumption.

• **Coal** is a **fossil fuel** that was formed over **millions of years** from the remains of dead plant matter buried under the earth. Once it is mined and burned, it cannot be replenished within a human timeframe.

• **Wind energy**, **Tidal energy**, and **Solar energy** are classified as **Renewable resources**. These sources are naturally replenished on a human timescale and are considered inexhaustible.

• The extraction and use of non-renewable resources like coal often lead to significant **environmental degradation** and the release of **greenhouse gases**.

**Additional Information__**

• Other major examples of **non-renewable resources** include **Petroleum (Oil)**, **Natural Gas**, and **Nuclear Energy** (specifically Uranium ore).

• **Renewable energy** is often referred to as **Clean Energy** because it generally produces lower levels of pollution compared to fossil fuels.

• The process of coal formation is known as **Coalification**, which involves the physical and chemical alteration of peat into lignite, sub-bituminous coal, bituminous coal, and finally **Anthracite**.

• Global efforts are currently focused on **Energy Transition**, moving away from non-renewable sources to mitigate the effects of **Climate Change**.
</ul

questions.question: What is the term for the economic phenomenon where high inflation is combined with stagnant economic growth?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Stagflation**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Stagflation** is an economic condition characterized by a combination of **stagnant economic growth**, **high unemployment**, and **high inflation**. This term is a portmanteau of **stagnation** and **inflation**.

• It is the correct answer because it specifically describes the phenomenon where **prices rise** (inflation) while the **economy slows down** (stagnation), which contradicts the traditional economic theory that inflation and unemployment have an inverse relationship.

• A **Recession** (Option 1) typically involves a significant decline in economic activity and **GDP**, but it is usually accompanied by low or falling **inflation** due to reduced consumer demand.

• **Hyperinflation** (Option 2) refers to an extremely rapid, out-of-control rise in **prices**, often exceeding **50% per month**, which can occur regardless of the growth state but usually leads to total economic collapse.

• **Deflation** (Option 4) is the opposite of **inflation**; it is a general decrease in the **price level** of goods and services, often leading to lower **consumer spending** as people wait for prices to drop further.

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Phillips Curve** is a historical economic concept developed by **A.W. Phillips**, suggesting that **inflation** and **unemployment** have a stable and inverse relationship. **Stagflation** in the **1970s** famously challenged this model.

• A **Supply Shock** is a primary cause of **stagflation**. For example, a sudden increase in the cost of **crude oil** raises production and transportation costs, leading to **cost-push inflation** and reduced **output**.

• The **Misery Index** is an economic indicator used to help determine how the average citizen is doing economically. It is calculated by adding the **seasonally adjusted unemployment rate** to the **annual inflation rate**.

• **Hyperinflation** has historically devastated economies, such as **Germany** in the **1920s** (Weimar Republic) and **Zimbabwe** in the **2000s**, where the **money supply** was increased excessively without corresponding **economic growth**.

• **Deflation** was a major feature of the **Great Depression** in the **1930s**, causing a **deflationary spiral** where falling prices led to lower production, lower wages, and higher **unemployment**.

**Important Points__**

• The term **Stagflation** was first coined by **Iain Macleod**, a **British politician** and **Chancellor of the Exchequer**, during a speech in the **House of Commons** in **1965**.

• The most famous global instance of **stagflation** occurred during the **1973 oil crisis**, when **OPEC** (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) imposed an oil embargo, causing **energy prices** to skyrocket and **industrial production** to plummet.

• For a **Central Bank** (such as the **RBI** in **India** or the **Federal Reserve** in the **USA**), **stagflation** is a policy nightmare. Raising **interest rates** to fight **inflation** can worsen **unemployment**, while lowering rates to stimulate **growth** can further fuel **inflation**.

• To resolve **stagflation**, economists often recommend **supply-side policies** that focus on increasing **productivity**, reducing **regulations**, and improving **infrastructure** to lower the cost of doing business.
</ul

questions.question: Which energy source cannot be replenished naturally in a short period of time?

The correct answer is __**Natural Gas**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Natural Gas** is classified as a **non-renewable energy source** because it takes millions of years to form from the remains of ancient marine organisms buried under layers of sediment and subjected to intense heat and pressure.

• Because the formation process of **fossil fuels** occurs over **geological timescales**, they cannot be replenished naturally in a short period of time once they are consumed.

• **Wind**, **Solar**, and **Hydroelectric** energy are **renewable resources**. These sources are constantly replenished by natural processes such as the **water cycle**, **solar radiation**, and **atmospheric circulation**.

• **Renewable energy** is considered sustainable because it is virtually inexhaustible on a human timeframe, unlike **finite resources** like natural gas, coal, and oil.

**Additional Information__**

• **Fossil fuels** (coal, petroleum, and natural gas) currently supply a large portion of the world's energy but are the primary drivers of **climate change** due to the emission of **carbon dioxide (CO2)** and other **greenhouse gases**.

• **Natural gas** is primarily composed of **methane (CH4)**. While it burns cleaner than coal, it is still a significant source of carbon emissions.

• The global shift toward **green energy** aims to replace non-renewable sources with **clean energy** alternatives like **geothermal**, **biomass**, and **tidal energy** to ensure **environmental sustainability**.

• **Energy conservation** and the use of **energy-efficient** technologies are also vital in reducing the rapid depletion of non-renewable resources.
</ul

questions.question: Name the principle that states that as production increases, the cost per unit decreases?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Economies of scale**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Economies of scale** refer to the cost advantage that a business experiences when it increases its level of **output**. The main reason for this is the inverse relationship between the **quantity of production** and **per-unit fixed costs**. As more units are produced, **fixed costs** like **rent**, **administrative salaries**, and **machinery depreciation** are spread over a larger volume, reducing the **average cost per unit**.

• **Law of diminishing returns**: This principle states that if one **factor of production** (like labor) is increased while others (like capital/land) are held **constant**, the **marginal output** will eventually decrease. This typically occurs in the **short-run** and leads to an **increase** in **marginal cost** rather than a decrease in unit cost. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• **Economies of scale**: This principle specifically describes the **long-run** phenomenon where increasing the **scale of production** leads to lower **average total costs**. This is achieved through **specialization**, **bulk purchasing** of **raw materials**, and **technological improvements**. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***

• **Opportunity cost**: This is the value of the **next best alternative** foregone when a choice is made. It is a fundamental concept in **resource allocation** but does not describe the relationship between **production volume** and **unit cost**. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• **Marginal utility**: This is an **economic concept** from the consumer side, representing the **additional satisfaction** or benefit a consumer derives from consuming one **additional unit** of a good or service. It generally **decreases** as consumption increases (**Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility**). ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Internal Economies of Scale**: These are internal to the **firm** and result from its own actions.

• **Technical Economies**: Large firms can afford **expensive** and **advanced machinery** that is more efficient.

• **Managerial Economies**: Large companies can hire **specialized managers** (e.g., **HR**, **Finance**, **Marketing**) to improve **operational efficiency**.

• **Financial Economies**: Large organizations often have better **credit ratings** and can borrow **capital** at **lower interest rates** compared to small businesses.

• **Marketing Economies**: The **advertising cost** per unit is lower for a firm producing **millions of units** compared to a small-scale producer.

• **External Economies of Scale**: These occur outside of an individual firm but within the **entire industry**.

• **Infrastructure**: If an industry grows in a specific **location**, the **government** may provide better **transportation** and **communication** links, benefiting all firms in that area.

• **Specialized Labor**: A large industry attracts a **skilled workforce**, reducing **recruitment** and **training costs** for individual companies.

• **Real-World Examples**: Companies like **Walmart** and **Amazon** utilize **economies of scale** by purchasing **inventory** in massive **bulk**, which allows them to negotiate **lower prices** from **suppliers** and pass those savings to **consumers**.

**Important Points__**

• **Diseconomies of Scale**: This happens when a **firm** grows so large that **average costs** begin to **increase**. This is often due to **communication failures**, **bureaucracy**, **lack of motivation** among workers, and **coordination problems** in very large **organizations**.

• **Adam Smith**: The concept of **economies of scale** was famously illustrated by **Adam Smith** in his **1776** book, **The Wealth of Nations**, using the example of a **pin factory** where **division of labor** significantly increased **productivity**.

• **Minimum Efficient Scale (MES)**: This is the **lowest point** on the **long-run average cost curve** where a firm can produce its **output** at the **minimum possible cost**. Reaching **MES** is crucial for **competitiveness** in **global markets**.

• **Fixed vs Variable Costs**: Understanding the difference is vital. **Fixed costs** (e.g., **insurance**, **rent**) do not change with **output**, while **variable costs** (e.g., **raw materials**, **direct labor**) change in direct **proportion** to the **volume** produced.
</ul

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Indus Valley Civilization (IVC)**, which flourished between **3300 BCE and 1300 BCE**, was an urban civilization whose economy was primarily based on a sophisticated **Barter system**.
 
• Despite their advanced urban planning and technical skills, the Harappans did not use **metallic coins** or any form of **currency-based economy**. Instead, goods were exchanged directly for other goods or services based on mutual requirements. ***Hence, the correct option is Barter system.***
 
• To facilitate this **Barter system**, the Harappans developed a highly standardized system of **weights and measures**. These weights were mostly cubical and made of a stone called **chert**.
 
• The system of weights followed a binary ratio for lower denominations (**1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, to 64**) and then shifted to a decimal system for higher values. The **measure of 16** was particularly significant in their daily transactions and remained a base for Indian currency (16 annas = 1 rupee) for centuries.
 
• Agricultural surplus was the foundation of this economy. The farmers produced enough **wheat**, **barley**, and **pulses** to support a large population of non-farmers, such as **artisans**, **merchants**, and **administrators**, who lived in planned cities like **Harappa** and **Mohenjo-daro**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Agriculture and Domestication**:

 
 
• The Harappans were the first people in the world to grow **cotton** (known as **Sindon** to the Greeks).
 
• Key crops included **wheat**, **barley**, **peas**, **sesame**, and **mustard**. Evidence of **rice** has been found specifically at **Lothal** and **Rangpur**.
 
• They domesticated animals like **oxen**, **buffaloes**, **goats**, **sheep**, and **pigs**. The **humped bull** was particularly favored.
 
 
 
• **Trade and Commerce**:
 
 
• The civilization had an extensive **maritime trade** network. **Lothal** in **Gujarat** served as a major **dockyard**, connecting the IVC to the **Persian Gulf** and **Mesopotamia**.
 
• Harappan **seals** (mostly made of **steatite**) have been discovered in **Mesopotamian** cities like **Susa** and **Ur**, proving international trade relations.
 
• Exports included **terracotta pots**, **beads** (from **Chanhudaro**), **ivory products**, and **cotton textiles**.
 
 
 
• **Craft and Technology**:
 
 
• The IVC is considered a **Bronze Age civilization**. They were proficient in making **bronze** by mixing **copper** (from **Khetri** mines in **Rajasthan**) with **tin** (from **Afghanistan**).
 
• They were experts in **bead-making**, **shell-cutting**, and **jewelry-making** using **gold**, **silver**, and semi-precious stones like **lapis lazuli** and **carnelian**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Seals as Identity**: While not used as currency, **seals** played a vital role in trade. They were used to stamp clay tags on sacks of goods to verify the **identity** of the sender and the **authenticity** of the contents.
 
• **Urban Infrastructure**: The economic prosperity is evident in the **Great Granary** found at **Mohenjo-daro**, which was used for storing grain—likely as a form of **state revenue** or emergency reserve.
 
• **Inland Transport**: For land-based trade, the Harappans used **bullock carts** and **pack animals**, while **river boats** were used for inland water transport along the **Indus River** and its tributaries.

questions.question: Who is the 15th President of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Droupadi Murmu**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Droupadi Murmu** assumed office as the **15th President of India** on **July 25, 2022**. She succeeded **Ram Nath Kovind** after winning the **2022 Presidential Election** as the nominee of the **National Democratic Alliance (NDA)**.
 
• She is the first person belonging to a **Scheduled Tribe** (specifically the **Santhal** community) to hold the highest constitutional office in the country. Her journey from the **Mayurbhanj** district of **Odisha** to **Rashtrapati Bhavan** is a significant milestone in Indian democracy.
 
• Born on **June 20, 1958**, she is the **youngest person** to ever hold the office of the President and the first to be born in **post-Independence India**.
 
• Before her presidency, she served as the **9th Governor of Jharkhand** from **2015 to 2021**, becoming the first woman governor of that state to complete a full five-year term.
 
• She is the **second woman** to serve as the President of India, following **Pratibha Patil**. ***Hence, the correct answer is Droupadi Murmu.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Pratibha Patil**:
 
 
• She served as the **12th President of India** from **2007 to 2012**.
 
• She holds the distinction of being the **first woman** to occupy the office of the President. Prior to this, she served as the **Governor of Rajasthan**.
 
 
 
• **Pranab Mukherjee**:
 
 
• He was the **13th President of India**, serving from **2012 to 2017**.
 
• A veteran statesman, he held various key portfolios in the Union Cabinet, including **Finance, Defence, and External Affairs**. He was posthumously awarded the **Bharat Ratna** in **2019**.
 
 
 
• **Ram Nath Kovind**:
 
 
• He served as the **14th President of India** from **2017 to 2022**.
 
• Before his tenure as President, he was the **Governor of Bihar**. He was the second **Dalit** president of India after **K. R. Narayanan**.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Role of the President**:
 
 
• The President is the **nominal head** of the executive, the **first citizen** of India, and the **Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces**.
 
• Under **Article 53** of the **Constitution of India**, the executive power of the Union is vested in the President and exercised either directly or through officers subordinate to them.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Article 52**: Explicitly states that "There shall be a **President of India**."
 
• **Article 54**: Defines the **Electoral College** for the election of the President, which includes elected members of both Houses of **Parliament** and the **Legislative Assemblies** of the States and Union Territories of **Delhi and Puducherry**.
 
• **Article 56**: Specifies the **term of office**, which is **five years** from the date the President enters upon their office.
 
• **Article 60**: Pertains to the **oath or affirmation** by the President, usually administered by the **Chief Justice of India**.
 
• **Article 61**: Outlines the procedure for **impeachment** if the President violates the Constitution.
</ul
